doc.title: Neal Caine interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, September 26, 2019

title: Life as a sideman and leader; whether to stay in music
summary: Music is fun but finances precarious; he has done trad, Elvin, Broadway and Harry Connick, considered quitting at 27 or 28, and doubts about jazz graduates' prospects.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: What is your — if you look at your calendar, look at a month in your calendar, as a person who plays as a sideman and then tries to find gigs as a leader. What’s it like to be a jazz musician and wear different hats? © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-

Well musically it’s fun and challenging. Financially it’s like walking a tightrope over a shark pit while juggling on roller skates. But I like the challenge. I’ve always liked, I’ve had a pretty wide career as far as different styles. Like I lived in New Orleans I played trad music; I played with Elvin; I’ve done you know a good amount of work on Broadway, which is a whole ‘nother world. So I’ve always liked the fact that I have had a diverse career. But you know it’s a bitch. I mean like you said, we were saying earlier, it’s very few bands that work like every day like the Basie — whatever. I’m lucky enough to work with Harry. But that’s only a certain amount of work a year, and then you’ve just got to freelance man, you’ve got to make it happen. It’s not for the weak. You’ve got to really love the music. I mean even now maybe even more so, because there’s less work. You’ve got to really be in it for the right reasons.

Well thank you for answering the question I didn’t ask and that was sort of what does a aspiring jazz musician need, assuming that they’re good players. And I think you’re saying that you have to just be so into it that you have to do it. Is that a fair statement?

I think so. I mean you know what, in my twenties there were times where — actually at one point I did kind of go I’m going to quit and go back to school. Like when I was maybe 27 or 8, because the travel and the whole thing. I mean but ultimately yeah, I had to do it. I was like this is for me, this really is for me. I have a lot of, I mean you know I was one of the young lions. So that was a time when it was kind of popular again and there was record deals. And there was a bunch of my friends from that era who were good players who, once that period kind of fell off and the realities of this life and the economic instability and you know they became — they did other things. And then some people stayed in it you know. And I think you just really have to love it.

I mean it’s still a decision — I don’t want to extend magical, I mean guys who were born to families with that stuff, that’s what they’re going to do. But it’s not like some magical thing where I had to do it, but ultimately it was the best decision.

Okay. If you look at jazz today and it’s thriving in academia, right? Every school, almost every school has a jazz program and summer camps and all that. It doesn’t seem to translate into the market, or into the club scene. I wonder what all of the jazz graduates do.

I don’t know. They become teachers. I don’t know man. I mean yeah, that’s a good question. I’m not sure. I didn’t go to, once again, I didn’t go to school. And I was lucky. I mean I was in the right place at the right time, and took advantage of it. But it’s tough out here. I mean if you look at the odds or are logical about it, yeah, it’s probably not a good industry to get into you know. © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-
